summary: Describes generic threats to routing protocols. It covers threat sources and capabilities, actions and consequences, and the harm attacks can do to users or the network. This is informational background for protocol designers.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes ways attackers can affect routing information and the traffic that depends on it. It provides a shared model of attackers, actions, and consequences rather than requirements for one routing protocol.

questions: what are the threats to routing protocols
what are the types of threat consequences
subtitle: A protocol-independent model of routing attack sources, actions, and consequences.

tldr.problem: Attacks on routing protocols can misdirect traffic, harm individual networks, or disrupt routing operations, but designers need a shared vocabulary for describing these threats.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes routing functions, attacker types and capabilities, four broad consequences, and threat actions such as spoofing, falsification, interference, and overload.
tldr.outcome: It is a protocol-independent threat analysis intended as a precursor to common security requirements for routing protocols.

today: RFC 4593 is an Informational RFC published in October 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It provides a protocol-independent threat analysis, not a set of routing requirements.

sections.title: Scope of the Threat Analysis
sections.content:
Routing protocols can be attacked in ways that harm individual users or network operations as a whole. This document summarizes generic routing threats, including their sources, actions, consequences, and the routing functions that can be attacked separately.

The analysis considers attacks against robust implementations of protocols such as OSPF, IS-IS, RIP, and BGP. It excludes bad or incomplete implementations and attacks against implementation-specific weaknesses.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sets out a general way to describe attacks on routing. It focuses on threats to well-designed protocols, not flaws in a particular implementation.

sections.title: Routing Functions at Risk
sections.content:
The RFC groups common routing functions into three parts: a transport subsystem for sending messages to neighbors, neighbor-state maintenance for establishing relationships, and database maintenance for exchanging topology and reachability information.

Some messages control protocol state, such as neighbor maintenance exchanges. Other messages carry routing information that affects how traffic is forwarded.
sections.plainLanguage: A routing protocol sends messages, maintains relationships with neighboring routers, and keeps routing information. An attack can target any of these functions.

sections.title: Attackers and Their Consequences
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes outsiders, who are not legitimate participants in the routing protocol, from Byzantine routers, which are faulty, misconfigured, or subverted legitimate participants. An outsider may spoof source addresses, observe or replay traffic, or modify messages in transit. A Byzantine router can send believable false information as a recognized participant.

Four broad consequences are disclosure of routing information, deception of a router into accepting a false message, disruption of a router's operation, and usurpation of services provided by a legitimate router. A single action can cause several consequences, and effects may persist until routes converge or network topology changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Threats can come from outsiders or from routers that participate but have gone wrong. They can expose routing information, mislead routers, interrupt routing, or take over a service.

sections.title: Scope and Duration of the Damage
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes damage to routing infrastructure from damage to a particular host or network. Infrastructure effects include congestion, blackholes, loops, partitions, churn, instability, excessive routing traffic, and resource exhaustion at a router. A targeted destination may instead experience starvation, eavesdropping, loss of reachability, delay, or looping.

The affected zone can range from one router or link to the global Internet. The period of impact depends on the action: effects may stop when the action stops, or persist until the routing system converges.
sections.plainLanguage: An attack can affect one destination or a much larger part of the network. Some effects end quickly, while others continue until routing information settles.

sections.title: Recognizable Threat Actions
sections.content:
The RFC identifies deliberate exposure, sniffing, and traffic analysis as ways to disclose routing information. Spoofing occurs when an illegitimate device assumes a legitimate identity; it can enable other attacks or prevent a genuine neighbor relationship from forming.

Falsification means sending false routing information. An originator may overclaim resources it does not control or misclaim resources in a way the administrator did not intend. A forwarder may change route attributes incorrectly, delete or insert data, substitute false data, or replay old information as current. Interference inhibits legitimate exchanges, while overload places excess burden on routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers may listen to routing exchanges, impersonate a router, or send false routes. They may also interrupt exchanges or burden routers with excess work.
